Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

make fun of verb

also poke fun at, mock, tease, laugh at, ridicule, he always makes fun of me, jeer, don’t laugh at him, don’t tease him, don’t laugh, rib, twit

classical

Plaut. Trin. 2.4.45: bonīs tuīs rēbus meās rēs irrīdēs malās (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 98: inrīdet

irrīdeō (inrīdeō), irrīdēre, irrīsī, irrīsum

verb, second conjugation, transitive

laugh at, mock

Other words

  • ēlūdō, ēlūdere, ēlūsī, ēlūsum — make sport of, make a fool of

    verb, third conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Cic. Ac. 2.39.123: et vōs ab illō irrīdēminī et ipsī illum vicissim ēlūditis (Lewis & Short); Traupman 98: iste mē semper ēlūdit

  • rīdeō, rīdēre, rīsī, rīsum + acc. — laugh at

    conjugation · also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 4.2.9: rīdeō hunc (Lewis & Short); Cic. Quinct. 55: rīdet nostram āmentiam (Lewis & Short); Traupman 33

    Milder than dērīdeō, says Lewis & Short: laughing at someone rather than jeering.

  • taxō, taxāre, taxāvī, taxātum — twit, taunt (someone) with a fault

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Suet. Aug. 4: Cassius Parmēnsis quādam epistulā sīc taxat Augustum (Lewis & Short); Traupman 33: don’t tease him, nōlī eum taxāre; Traupman 370

    Lewis & Short: “to twit, censure, reproach, charge with a fault”; in Suetonius a letter taunts Augustus with his humble ancestry, which is mockery with a sting. A post-Augustan word (Suetonius, Pliny); for good-natured teasing, rīdēre or irrīdēre. See also criticism.

Examples

  • Iste mē semper ēlūdit.

    He always makes fun of me.Traupman 98

  • Nōlī (nōlīte) rīdēre eum (eam).

    Don’t laugh at him (her).Traupman 33

  • Iste mē semper ēlūdit (inrīdet).

    He always makes fun of me.Traupman 319

See also joke, laugh.

SourcesQuotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
